evidence.title: Aligning Evaluation to Deployment: Measuring the Clinical Utility of End-to-End Deep Learning for Lung Cancer Screening
evidence.outcome: Whether aggregate AUC vs subgroup calibration and operating-point metrics reveal model performance differences
evidence.effect: Models had similar AUCs (year-1 0.91–0.95) but calibration varied by Lung-RADS category; under-predicted at highest-risk tier (11% predicted vs 22% observed), which aggregate metrics concealed.
evidence.quote: Calibration was good in aggregate but varied by category: the models over-predicted in the low-risk Lung-RADS tiers, were well calibrated at intermediate risk, and under-predicted in the high-risk tiers where workup is decided (11% predicted against 22% observed at the highest-risk tier).
evidence.sample_unit: LDCT scans (2,199 patients) from NLST test cohort

evidence.title: OSAIRIS: Lessons Learned From the Hospital-Based Implementation and Evaluation of an Open-Source Deep-Learning Model for Radiotherapy Image Segmentation
evidence.venue: Clinical oncology (Royal College of Radiologists (Great Britain))
evidence.outcome: metric correlation with editing time
evidence.effect: Hausdorff distance best correlated with editing-time, outperforming dice, with Spearman 0.70 and Kendall 0.52.
evidence.quote: Combining editing time data with accuracy metrics, we found the Hausdorff distance best correlated with editing-time, outperforming dice, the industry-standard, with a Spearman correlation coefficient of 0.70, and a Kendall coefficient of 0.52.

evidence.title: Accounting for inconclusive results and repeated testing: A framework for evaluating wearable electrocardiogram diagnostic performance with application to Apple Watch and artificial intelligence-enhanced interpretation
evidence.outcome: AF sensitivity/specificity under naive, pragmatic, and intention-to-diagnose reporting frameworks
evidence.effect: Apple Watch naive 96.1%/97.9%, pragmatic 78.1%/81.0%, ITD 92.2%/91.0%; naive reporting excluding inconclusive results inflates performance, pragmatic deflates it.
evidence.quote: Apple Watch naive sensitivity/specificity were 96.1%/97.9%; pragmatic 78.1%/81.0%; ITD 92.2%/91.0%.

evidence.title: External Validation of an Artificial Intelligence Triaging System for Chest X-Rays: A Retrospective Independent Clinical Study
evidence.outcome: Comparison of ensemble decision thresholds/strategies and their sensitivity-specificity tradeoffs
evidence.effect: Four ensemble strategies compared; sensitivity-prioritized methods reached sensitivity >0.92 but specificity <0.69, while the weighted ensemble gave the best balance.
evidence.quote: Sensitivity-prioritized methods achieving sensitivity >0.92 produced lower specificity (<0.69).

evidence.title: Evaluation of segmentation accuracy and the improvement of time effectiveness using deep learning-based segmentation in 177Lu-DOTATATE dosimetry
evidence.outcome: Output-appropriate contour metrics
evidence.effect: DSC and MDA met thresholds, but HD was approximately 20.0 mm in liver and spleen.
evidence.quote: In our study, DSC and MDA met the tolerance threshold in the liver and spleen, but HD was approximately 20.0 mm.

evidence.title: Multi-label arrhythmia classification from Holter scatter plots using deep learning and clinically oriented thresholds
evidence.outcome: Effect of clinically oriented label-specific thresholds versus fixed 0.5 threshold on specificity and macro-F1
evidence.effect: Clinically oriented thresholds increased mean specificity from 0.844 (0.822–0.865) to 0.885 (0.860–0.909), but reduced macro-F1 to 0.693 (0.628–0.726) from 0.738.
evidence.quote: Clinically oriented thresholds increased mean specificity from 0.844 (0.822–0.865) to 0.885 (0.860–0.909), but reduced macro-F1 to 0.693 (0.628–0.726).

evidence.title: When external validation isn’t enough: Simpson’s paradox, direction asymmetry, and calibration collapse in cross-continental perioperative mortality prediction
evidence.outcome: Subgroup discrimination metrics
evidence.effect: Simpson’s paradox gap range 5.0–16.5 pp; worst aggregate AUC 0.756 vs within-stratum AUCs 0.58–0.60.
evidence.quote: Across the eight cross-population runs, aggregate AUCs concealed substantially lower within-stratum AUCs (Simpson’s paradox gap range 5.0–16.5 pp; worst case: aggregate AUC 0.756 vs within-stratum AUCs 0.58–0.60).

evidence.title: Demographic shortcuts as marker-free backdoors: silent subgroup underdiagnosis that only operating-point audits detect
evidence.outcome: Ability of threshold-based subgroup metrics versus rank-based metrics to detect subgroup underperformance
evidence.effect: Subgroup false-negative rate audit at deployed threshold flagged 96% of installed failures vs 73% for rank-based audit; overall AUROC moved only 0.004.
evidence.quote: What works is auditing subgroup false-negative rate at the deployed threshold, which flagged 96% of installed failures compared to 73% for a rank-based audit.

evidence.title: Defining operational safety in clinical artificial intelligence systems
evidence.outcome: Whether AUC alone versus reliability-based operational metrics distinguishes model safety
evidence.effect: Models with nearly identical AUC 0.960 had Gray Zone Areas of 0.709 vs 0.344; the higher-AUC FDA-cleared model was less safe for high-confidence rule-out.
evidence.quote: This result shows that the AUC can be misleading and that models should be evaluated for their operational safety to understand their true clinical utility.

evidence.title: Continuous Evaluation Frameworks for Retrospective Evaluation of Clinical Machine Learning Models
evidence.outcome: Whether continuous evaluation frameworks reveal performance differences missed by single time point metrics such as AUROC
evidence.effect: Models with high AUROC showed markedly different performance under continuous evaluation across both datasets; no numbers reported in the abstract.
evidence.quote: Across both datasets, models with high AUROC demonstrate markedly different performance when continuously evaluated.

evidence.title: Organ Segmentation with Machine Learning Models
evidence.outcome: Whether per-organ Dice, HD95 and surface Dice reveal model differences hidden by aggregate Dice
evidence.effect: Rankings reshuffle by 10-13% on small, complex organs; boundary fidelity separates models into tiers that the Dice ranking hides; aggregate Dice alone judged unsafe for selection.
evidence.quote: Selecting a model on aggregate Dice alone is therefore unsafe for organ-specific clinical tasks: per-organ overlap and boundary metrics should be the primary acceptance criteria for selecting a model before clinical deployment.
evidence.sample_unit: CT scans (AMOS training/evaluation; TotalSegmentator external set)

evidence.title: Integrating Clinical Priorities into the Technical Validation of Machine Learning Classifiers: A Generalizable Framework Demonstrated on Opioid Misuse Screening
evidence.outcome: Whether clinically weighted metrics, CIs, and threshold choice change model ranking versus raw accuracy
evidence.effect: Raw accuracy ranked CSBT-Untuned highest (0.867) but it detected only 38.5% of misuse cases; balanced accuracy/CDPS ranked CSBT-Tuned highest (0.696). Bootstrap CIs showed CSBT-Tuned and RUSBoost overlap.
evidence.quote: WEAS reversed this ordering, ranking CSBT-Tuned highest (0.696), followed by RUSBoost (0.690) and CSBT-Untuned (0.658).
evidence.sample_unit: survey respondents in the held-out test set (NSDUH 2015-2019)

evidence.title: Intelligent fall risk prediction and real-time warning system for elderly care based on multimodal deep learning and wearable sensor fusion
evidence.outcome: Overall accuracy masking poor high-risk classification under extreme class imbalance
evidence.effect: Reported accuracy was 94.2%, versus 97.98% for always-low-risk predictions. High-risk PPV was 6.25%; sensitivity was 83.3% (5/6), with one misclassification shifting sensitivity by approximately 17% points.
evidence.quote: A classifier that predicted “low risk” for every window would achieve 97.98% accuracy, which is actually higher than our model’s overall figure—the difference being that our model trades some majority-class accuracy for improved sensitivity to minority-class events, as intended by the focal loss objective.

evidence.title: Closed-Loop Quality Assurance for Production Clinical AI Documentation
evidence.outcome: Correlation of binary check scores with physician preference
evidence.effect: Notes scoring 90%+ on binary checks were rejected by physicians; ρ = −0.077, p = 0.652, n = 36.
evidence.quote: Second, the same binary check instrument produces opposite outcomes depending on how it is used: as an optimization target, it yields notes scoring 90%+ that physicians reject (  ρ = −0.077,  p = 0.652,  n = 36; not statistically significant); as a deployment gate asking “did this specific fabrication stop?”, it provides rater-invariant commit decisions.

evidence.title: Benefit-Risk Reporting for FDA-Cleared Artificial Intelligence-Enabled Medical Devices
evidence.outcome: Reporting of sensitivity and specificity performance metrics in premarket summaries
evidence.effect: Sensitivity reported for 166 (24.0%) and specificity for 152 (22.0%) devices.
evidence.quote: Few premarket summaries contained data published in peer-reviewed journals (272 [39.4%]) or provided statistical or clinical performance, including sensitivity (166 [24.0%]), specificity (152 [22.0%]), and/or patient outcomes (3 [<1%]).

evidence.title: Prospective Validation of a Suicide Event Risk Model in Transgender Patients
evidence.venue: AMIA ... Annual Symposium proceedings. AMIA Symposium
evidence.outcome: Calibration of the model in the transgender subgroup
evidence.effect: Significant miscalibration: Brier=0.023, Spiegelhalter's z-statistic p<0.001, despite modest discrimination (AUROC=0.777).
evidence.quote: Results indicated modest discriminative ability (AUROC=0.777, AUPRC=0.115), however, a high rate of false negatives (77%), and significant miscalibration (Brier=0.023, Spiegelhalter's z-statistic p<0.001) reduced clinical utility.

evidence.title: AI-based disease severity grading predicts complications in laparoscopic appendectomy
evidence.outcome: Model discrimination (AUC), calibration and decision curve net benefit for predicting complications
evidence.effect: AI severity AUC 0.63 vs operative-AAST 0.68; calibration acceptable at extremes and improved at intermediate risk; DCA highest net benefit at intermediate risk.
evidence.quote: Discrimination was modest (AUC = 0.63), similar to operative-AAST (AUC = 0.68).

evidence.title: Not What the Doctor Ordered: Surveying LLM-based De-identification and Quantifying Clinical Information Loss
evidence.outcome: Adequacy of evaluation metrics for detecting clinical information removal in LLM de-identification
evidence.effect: Traditional classification metrics are inadequate for LLM errors that alter clinical information; an existing metric was manually validated by clinical experts and showed poor performance.
evidence.quote: We highlight poor performance and describe the inherent limitations of such metrics in identifying clinically significant changes.

evidence.title: WER is Unaware: Assessing How ASR Errors Distort Clinical Understanding in Patient Facing Dialogue
evidence.outcome: Correlation of WER and other ASR metrics with clinician-assigned clinical risk labels
evidence.effect: WER and a comprehensive suite of existing metrics correlated poorly with clinician-assigned risk labels (No, Minimal, Significant Impact); the optimized LLM judge reached 90% accuracy and Cohen's kappa 0.816.
evidence.quote: Our analysis reveals that WER and a comprehensive suite of existing metrics correlate poorly with the clinician-assigned risk labels (No, Minimal, or Significant Impact).

evidence.title: Preferred, Not Safer: Pairwise Preference Is a Poor Proxy for Clinical Safety
evidence.outcome: Whether pairwise preference metric reflects clinical safety performance of LLMs
evidence.effect: Preference is a poor proxy for safety; highly ranked models still had substantial rates of clinically meaningful failures (<= -1), and surface features explained slightly more preference variation than safety rubric differences.
evidence.quote: we find that clinician preference is a poor proxy for safety-critical performance.

evidence.title: TOWARDS AN AI-DRIVEN REGISTRY FOR POSTOPERATIVE COMPLICA-TIONS: A PROOF-OF-CONCEPT STUDY EVALUATING THE OPPORTUNITIES AND CHALLENGES OF AI-MODELS
evidence.outcome: Effect of decision threshold choice (F0.5 vs F2) on detected complication rates and hospital comparisons
evidence.effect: NLP models detected 8,512 or 15,892 PCs depending on threshold, total PC rates 9.14% vs 17.1%; threshold selection significantly influenced findings and hospital comparisons.
evidence.quote: Regression analyses demonstrated that threshold se-lection significantly influenced findings, impacting hospital comparisons.

evidence.title: Large-Language-Model Mortality Risk Stratification in the Intensive Care Unit: A Benchmark Against APACHE II
evidence.outcome: Calibration of LLM mortality risk categories versus APACHE II predictions
evidence.effect: LLMs overestimated risk, classifying more patients as high risk than APACHE II; mortality in high-risk groups was lower than APACHE-predicted rates, indicating calibration mismatch.
evidence.quote: Mortality rates within high-risk groups were lower than APACHE-predicted rates, suggesting calibration mismatch.

evidence.title: Calibration Drift Under Cross-Institutional Deployment: An External Validation Framework for ICU Mortality Prediction Across MIMIC-IV and eICU
evidence.outcome: External calibration underperformance
evidence.effect: External validation revealed systematic risk overestimation (intercept −0.678) after near-ideal internal calibration.
evidence.quote: Internal calibration was near-ideal (slope 0.982; intercept 0.001), whereas external validation revealed systematic risk overestimation (intercept − 0.678) attributable to prevalence-driven label shift.

evidence.title: Evaluating medical AI models beyond predictive performance: a diabetic retinopathy screening case study
evidence.outcome: Probability calibration of DR models on external datasets (Expected Calibration Error)
evidence.effect: Despite median AUROC 0.974 (0.904–0.993), calibration was poor (ECE 0.031–0.133).
evidence.quote: Model calibration was poor (Expected Calibration Error; 0.031–0.133), and estimated uncertainty did not align with clinicians' assessments (Pearson's r ; 0.156–0.548).
evidence.country: multi-country (six external fundus datasets; HMADR_Clinic clinic dataset)

evidence.title: Ranking-optimized survival models can underperform fixed-horizon clinical prediction
evidence.outcome: Concordance index versus timepoint-specific discrimination as evaluation metrics
evidence.effect: Concordance was competitive (0.705) but 60-day AUROC was 0.750, below comparators (0.808, 0.827); recalibration did not change discrimination.
evidence.quote: The survival model achieved a competitive ranking concordance (0.705) but underperformed both comparators at fixed horizons: at 60 days its area under the ROC curve was 0.750, versus 0.808 for physicians (on the matched sample) and 0.827 for the 1995 model, a gap reproduced across eight independent splits and statistically reliable after multiplicity correction.

evidence.title: External Validation and Calibration Assessment of Explainable Machine Learning Models for GVHD Prediction After Allogeneic HSCT
evidence.outcome: calibration drift
evidence.effect: Negative calibration intercept in 10 of 11 evaluable external cohort-target combinations; heterogeneous slope drift required cohort-specific recalibration.
evidence.quote: Calibration analysis identified systematic external risk overestimation (negative calibration intercept in 10 of 11 evaluable external cohort-target combinations) with heterogeneous slope drift requiring cohort-specific recalibration.
evidence.country: United States, UAE, Jordan (multi-country registry cohorts)

evidence.title: Trustworthy personalized treatment selection: causal effect-trees and calibration in perioperative medicine
evidence.outcome: Subgroup calibration error of effect-tree treatment recommendations
evidence.effect: Four of five subgroups had calibration error < 0.08; one small subgroup (N=250) had calibration error 0.44, flagged as unreliable.
evidence.quote: Calibration analysis identified four of five subgroups as reliable for deployment (calibration error < 0.08), while one small subgroup (N=250) showed higher calibration error (0.44), illustrating how the framework rates unreliable heterogeneity.

evidence.title: Class imbalance correction in artificial intelligence models leads to miscalibrated clinical predictions: a real-world evaluation
evidence.outcome: Calibration (log loss, over-prediction) versus discrimination (AUROC/AUPRC) after class imbalance correction
evidence.effect: Correction methods did not improve AUROC or AUPRC but severely compromised calibration, with risk over-prediction up to 62.8% and increased log loss across all mitigation techniques.
evidence.quote: However, these methods severely compromised model calibration, leading to significant over-prediction of risks (up to a 62.8 % increase) as further evidenced by increased log loss across all mitigation techniques.

evidence.title: Cardiovascular risk scores for primary prevention: head-to-head validation of 16 established and contemporary models
evidence.outcome: Whether discrimination alone reflects calibration and clinical utility of risk models
evidence.effect: AUC ranged 0.668 to 0.734 while calibration varied substantially and net benefit diverged at higher treatment thresholds; QRISK2 had best calibration, PREVENT lowest Brier score.
evidence.quote: Model selection for primary prevention should require external validation, local recalibration, and assessment of clinical utility, rather than reliance on discrimination alone.

evidence.title: Local-First Clinical Text Structuring with Fine-Tuned MedGemma for Readmission Risk Assessment
evidence.outcome: Calibration of readmission risk probabilities from A3 model
evidence.effect: Predicted probabilities over-confident in higher-risk bins; A3 calibration slope 0.741; pre-deployment recalibration needed.
evidence.quote: Because predicted probabilities are over-confident in higher-risk bins (A3 calibration slope 0.741), pre-deployment recalibration is a prerequisite for any probability-based clinical use.
evidence.sample_unit: patients (MIMIC-IV admissions cohort; test split n=9,857)

evidence.title: Selective prediction as a triage gate for primary-care depression screening: quantifying and mitigating selection bias in CHARLS-2011
evidence.outcome: Calibration trajectory across selection levels
evidence.effect: AUC rose with selection but not after multiple-comparison correction, whereas calibration error increased for four of five models.
evidence.quote: AUC rose with selection but not after multiple-comparison correction, whereas calibration error increased for four of five models.

evidence.title: Evaluating Methods for Assessing LLM-Translated Clinical Discharge Instructions: A Comparison of Automated Metrics, MQM-Based Evaluation, and Clinician Review
evidence.outcome: LLM judge agreement with clinicians
evidence.effect: LLM-based MQM scoring and clinician assessment had generally slight agreement (κ = −0.18 to 0.20).
evidence.quote: Agreement between LLM-based MQM scoring and clinician assessment was generally slight across domains (κ = −0.18 to 0.20), whereas inter-rater agreement between clinicians ranged from slight to moderate (κ = −0.11 to 0.49), highlighting the inherent subjectivity of clinical translation assessment.

evidence.title: Explainable Machine Learning and Temporal Calibration Drift of a TyG- BMI-Based Model for Early Prediction of Gestational Diabetes Mellitus
evidence.outcome: calibration despite stable discrimination
evidence.effect: Calibration changed despite preserved discrimination; intercept shifts XGBoost Δintercept −0.866 and LightGBM −0.977.
evidence.quote: Calibration changed over time: calibration intercepts shifted downward from the internal holdout to the temporal cohort (XGBoost Δintercept − 0.866; LightGBM − 0.977), indicating increasing average overprediction under the offset-model definition of calibration-in-the-large, a directionally consistent shift seen across all three models (though with wide confidence intervals), while discrimination was largely preserved.

evidence.title: Development and External Validation of a Treatment-Adjusted Machine Learning Model to Support Risk-Informed Group-Based Depression Care for People Living with HIV in Uganda
evidence.outcome: Calibration before Platt recalibration
evidence.effect: Platt recalibration improved Brier score from 0.174 to 0.113 and calibration slope from 7.533 to 1.093.
evidence.quote: Following Platt-recalibration, XGBoost showed the best overall performance, preserving strong discrimination (AUC 0.940) while improving the Brier score from 0.174 to 0.113 and the calibration slope from 7.533 to 1.093.
evidence.sample_unit: adults living with HIV with significant depression symptoms

evidence.title: Silent calibration drift in a frozen clinical prediction model: a decade-long audit and an operational monitoring framework
evidence.outcome: Discrimination-only validation missed calibration drift
evidence.effect: AUC stayed 0.76, 0.74, and 0.75, but calibration intercepts drifted to −0.54 and −0.31; both 95% CIs excluded zero.
evidence.quote: Discrimination remained stable (optimism-corrected development AUC 0.76; later eras 0.74 and 0.75), but calibration drifted: the intercept became − 0.54 and − 0.31, both 95% CIs excluding zero, with over-prediction in both access strata.

evidence.title: External validation reveals poor calibration despite preserved discrimination for a vasopressin treatment-signal prediction model across ICU databases
evidence.outcome: Calibration under preserved discrimination
evidence.effect: Internal calibration slope 1.501 (under-dispersed) despite CITL 0.007; external CITL −0.712 with slope 0.446; external AUROC 0.746.
evidence.quote: Mean overprediction (calibration-in-the-large − 0.712) occurred with a slope of 0.446.
evidence.sample_unit: ICU stays (3,692 training, 1,582 MIMIC-IV internal test, 1,801 eICU-CRD external)

evidence.title: The impact of evaluation strategy on sepsis prediction model performance metrics in intensive care data
evidence.outcome: Variation of performance metrics across evaluation strategies (fixed horizon, peak score, continuous) on the same model and data
evidence.effect: Same model and dataset gave different AUROCs by strategy; fixed horizon AUROC was 0.61 (0.60–0.62) versus about 0.67 for continuous; peak score similar to continuous; metrics improved with shorter horizons.
evidence.quote: Our results demonstrate that the choice of evaluation strategy has a significant impact on the performance metrics of intensive care prediction models.

evidence.title: A recalibrated prediction model can identify level-1 trauma patients at risk of nosocomial pneumonia
evidence.venue: Archives of orthopaedic and trauma surgery
evidence.outcome: Discrimination-calibration mismatch
evidence.effect: Despite AUC 0.83 (95% CI 0.79 – 0.87), calibration was poor: slope 0.63 and mean predicted risk 6.4% vs. 10.6% observed.
evidence.quote: The original model showed good discriminatory capacity (AUC 0.83, 95% CI 0.79 – 0.87) but was overfitted for use in the Dutch population (calibration slope 0.63; mean predicted risk 6.4% vs. 10.6% observed risk).

evidence.title: Validation in Indonesia of two published scores for mortality prediction after cardiac surgery
evidence.outcome: poor calibration despite discrimination
evidence.effect: EuroSCORE II AUC 0.774 (0.714–0.834), but HL P < 0.001 and mortality underestimated 2.1% predicted versus 3.8% observed.
evidence.quote: The EuroSCORE II, despite good discrimination, showed poor calibration.

evidence.title: Adjusting FRAX Estimates of Fracture Probability Based on a Positive Vertebral Fracture Assessment
evidence.outcome: FRAX calibration in VFA-positive patients
evidence.effect: With prior clinical fracture and positive VFA, FRAX underestimated MOF risk by 53% and hip fracture risk by 76%.
evidence.quote: In these individuals, FRAX underestimated MOF risk by 53% (recalibration multiplier: 1.53) and hip fracture risk by 76% (recalibration multiplier: 1.76).

evidence.title: Performance of Machine Learning Suicide Risk Models in an American Indian Population
evidence.outcome: Calibration of models applied to new population
evidence.effect: Spiegelhalter z scores -89.9 (VU) and 15.5 (MHRN), P<.001, indicating poor calibration despite reasonable AUROC.
evidence.quote: For the outcome of 90-day suicide attempts, the Spiegelhalter z score was −89.9 ( P < .001) for the VU model and 15.5 ( P < .001) for the MHRN primary care model.

evidence.title: Clinical prediction models for patients undergoing total hip arthroplasty: an external validation based on a systematic review and the Dutch Arthroplasty Register
evidence.outcome: Calibration reporting in development papers of published models
evidence.effect: Development papers did not present calibration plots, so calibration could not be compared; discrimination was similar between cohorts but calibration poor in validation.
evidence.quote: Calibration plots were not presented in the development papers, and therefore could not be compared.

evidence.title: Evaluating Large Language Model-Supported Instructions for Medication Use: First Steps Toward a Comprehensive Model
evidence.outcome: Automated similarity missed errors
evidence.effect: A 94.75% similarity rate still coincided with partial inadequacy and error types 5, 6, and 7.
evidence.quote: For instance, directions for spiramycin prescribed to a pregnant woman achieved a similarity rate of 94.75% with prompt 1 ( Table 3 ) despite being partially inadequate and containing error types 5, 6, and 7 (hallucinations) as identified by specialists ( Table 2 ).

evidence.title: Evaluating large language models in echocardiography reporting: opportunities and challenges
evidence.outcome: Correlation of automatic metrics with cardiologist ratings and sensitivity to changed measurement numbers
evidence.effect: Automatic-human metric correlations were fair to modest (best RadGraph F1 vs clinical utility r = 0.42); automatic metrics showed only 0-5% drop when measurement numbers were changed.
evidence.quote: automatic metrics showed insensitivity (0-5% drop) to changes in measurement numbers

evidence.title: Optimizing Artificial Intelligence Thresholds for Mammographic Lesion Detection: A Retrospective Study on Diagnostic Performance and Radiologist-Artificial Intelligence Discordance
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity at a single AI threshold (35) by BI-RADS subgroup
evidence.effect: At threshold 35, sensitivity for BI-RADS 4A was 41.2% (specificity 84.7%) versus 88.7% sensitivity (specificity 70.2%) for 4B/C, showing a single threshold conceals subgroup underperformance.
evidence.quote: At a threshold of 35, the sensitivity for BI-RADS 4A cases was only 41.2%, with a specificity of 84.7%.

evidence.title: Qualitative evaluation of automatic liver segmentation in computed tomography images for clinical use in radiation therapy
evidence.venue: Cancer radiotherapie : journal de la Societe francaise de radiotherapie oncologique
evidence.outcome: Agreement between geometric metrics (Dice, Hausdorff) and clinician acceptability ratings
evidence.effect: Dice and Hausdorff do not always align with clinician assessment; some high-Dice segmentations still required clinician corrections before clinical use.
evidence.quote: In some cases, segmentations with high Dice scores still required clinician corrections before clinical use in the radiotherapy workflow.

evidence.title: External Validation of Mortality Prediction Models in Japanese Transcatheter Aortic Valve Replacement Registry
evidence.venue: European journal of cardio-thoracic surgery : official journal of the European Association for Cardio-thoracic Surgery
evidence.outcome: Short-term model calibration
evidence.effect: All short-term MPMs overestimated mortality risk despite top AU-ROCs of 0.82 and 0.78.
evidence.quote: Among short-term MPMs, NHR (AU-ROC: 0.82) and STS-PRoM (0.78) showed the highest discrimination, though all models overestimated mortality risk, which improved after intercept recalibration.

evidence.title: Challenges and Strategies for Deep Learning in Cardiovascular Imaging: Ejection Fraction and Heart Failure Management
evidence.outcome: Reliability of AUC as evaluation metric for dichotomized heart failure diagnosis
evidence.effect: AUC varied from 0.71 to 0.98 owing solely to changes in population characteristics, showing significant unreliability of the AUC.
evidence.quote: Specifically, AUC varied from 0.71 to 0.98 owing solely to changes in population characteristics.

evidence.title: Evaluating the impact of data biases on algorithmic fairness and clinical utility of machine learning models for prolonged opioid use prediction
evidence.outcome: Calibration and subgroup miscalibration in external validation
evidence.effect: Model overestimates higher probabilities, and underestimates probabilities below 0.6 in opioid-exposed subgroup in Stage 2; depression and opioid-exposed showed most miscalibration.
evidence.quote: This situation varies in the opioid-exposed subgroup, where the model underestimates probabilities below 0.6 in Stage 2.

evidence.title: Digital Pathology with AI for Cervical Biopsies: Diagnostic Accuracy at the CIN2+ Threshold
evidence.outcome: Justification of decision threshold for AI slide-level positivity
evidence.effect: The ≥15-tile operating point was chosen heuristically, not from ROC or decision-curve analysis; no continuous score or tunable operating point.
evidence.quote: The threshold was not derived from formal ROC or decision-curve calibration and is therefore reported as a methodological limitation.

evidence.title: Benchmarking robustness of automated CT pancreas segmentation: achieving human-level reliability through human-in-the-loop optimization
evidence.outcome: Robustness hidden by mean metrics
evidence.effect: Even best models lacked robustness: 5% to 7% of predictions fell below minimum performance threshold despite high mean metrics.
evidence.quote: Our multireader evaluation revealed that even the best-performing pancreas segmentation models lacked robustness: 5% to 7% of predictions fell below the minimum performance threshold in cases that human readers handled consistently.
evidence.sample_unit: test CT scans (each with 4 independent human segmentations)

evidence.title: Evaluating Medical Text Summaries Using Automatic Evaluation Metrics and LLM-as-a-Judge Approach: A Pilot Study
evidence.outcome: Automatic metric detection of hallucinations
evidence.effect: Hallucinations Spearman coefficients were ROUGE-1 0.17, ROUGE-2 0.10, ROUGE-L 0.19, BLEU 0.11, METEOR 0.14, BERTScore 0.23.
evidence.quote: The expectedly low correlation between the automatic evaluation metrics and the expert scores provides evidence of their infeasibility as reliable independent evaluators.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries (30 EHR documents x 6 LLMs)

evidence.title: Foundation models enable wearable signal screening for cardiovascular disease among people living with HIV
evidence.outcome: Discordance between AUROC and operating-threshold sensitivity
evidence.effect: With ECG embeddings, LightGBM achieved AUROC 0.756 ± 0.10 but recall 0.000 ± 0.00 and Balanced Accuracy 0.500 ± 0.00; XGBoost showed a similar pattern.
evidence.quote: In contrast, tree ensembles frequently exhibited a small- n failure mode: LightGBM attained a high AUROC (0.756 ± 0.10) but defaulted to no positive calls (recall 0.000 ± 0.00; Balanced Accuracy 0.500 ± 0.00), with a similar pattern for XGBoost.

evidence.title: Artificial Intelligence-powered tiered early warning framework addressing high false alarm rates for in-hospital mortality prediction
evidence.outcome: Low PPV under class imbalance
evidence.effect: At Youden thresholds, PPVs were 13.9% in H1, 11.0% in H2, and 9.8% in H3.
evidence.quote: However, PPVs remained low (13.9% in H1, 11.0% in H2, and 9.8% in H3), revealing a high false positive burden under realistic deployment conditions.

evidence.title: AI-assisted tumor board decision-making in pancreatic oncology
evidence.venue: BMC medical informatics and decision making
evidence.outcome: Whether aggregate accuracy conceals poor category-specific performance
evidence.effect: Overall accuracy of 78.6% masked zero recall for neoadjuvant candidates (0/7); aggregate metrics hid a critical class-specific failure.
evidence.quote: The high global accuracy masks a significant safety limitation regarding the recognition of complex, intermediate-stage patients.
evidence.sample_unit: tumor board cases (first-diagnosis pancreatic cancer patients)

evidence.title: The Impact of Evaluation Strategy on Sepsis Prediction Model Performance Metrics in Intensive Care Data: Retrospective Cohort Study
evidence.outcome: Variation in AUROC across evaluation strategies for the same model and dataset
evidence.effect: Fixed horizon AUROC 0.61 (95% CI 0.60-0.62) versus about 0.67 for continuous and peak score evaluation; metrics improved with shorter horizons.
evidence.quote: The same model applied to the same dataset yields markedly different performance metrics depending on the evaluation approach.

evidence.title: Performance of clinical breast cancer risk prediction models vs a mammography-based artificial intelligence risk model
evidence.venue: Journal of the National Cancer Institute
evidence.outcome: Discrimination versus calibration of AI risk model, including calibration by risk stratum
evidence.effect: MIRAI C-index 0.71 for overall and invasive cancer, higher than clinical models (0.59-0.68), yet it overestimated risk in low-risk women (about 50%) and for invasive cancer.
evidence.quote: However, for low-risk women (approximately 50%), MIRAI overestimated risk of overall breast cancer.
evidence.sample_unit: women in a screening mammography cohort

evidence.title: Structural error asymmetry and harm-weighted analysis of ChatGPT versus ICU Physicians in acid-base interpretation: a prospective observational study
evidence.outcome: Harm-weighted severity of misclassification errors, ChatGPT vs physicians
evidence.effect: Significantly higher clinical severity of errors for ChatGPT (mean difference 0.12; 95% CI 0.032–0.220; p = 0.026), despite comparable aggregate accuracy.
evidence.quote: Harm-weighted misclassification modeling showed significantly higher clinical severity of errors for ChatGPT (mean difference 0.12; 95% CI 0.032–0.220; p = 0.026).
evidence.sample_unit: consecutive ICU patients' arterial blood gas interpretations

evidence.title: Key aspects of fine-tuning and applying LLM-as-a-judge for clinical data summaries in the radiological workflow
evidence.outcome: automatic metric validity for medical summaries
evidence.effect: ROUGE-1 0.29–0.38, BLEU 0.06–0.12, BERTScore 0.72–0.77; authors judged automated metrics poorly applicable.
evidence.quote: The results presented in Table 4 indicate that automated metrics are poorly applicable to our task.
evidence.sample_unit: LLM-generated summaries of EHRs (30 patients, 6 summarizing LLMs)

evidence.title: Improving patient understanding of oncology imaging: radiologist and patient evaluation of summarised versus full-length AI-simplified reports from a tertiary cancer centre
evidence.venue: Cancer imaging : the official publication of the International Cancer Imaging Society
evidence.outcome: Cohort-stratified versus pooled performance
evidence.effect: Lung favored A (factual correctness P=0.001; completeness P<0.0001); colorectal favored B (all P<0.002); combined medians did not differ (all p>0.057).
evidence.quote: The differences in both cancer cohorts are cancelled when combined, a possible case of Simpson’s paradox [ 17 ], hence the importance of analysing the cohorts separately.
evidence.sample_unit: original CT oncology reports (30 colorectal, 30 lung), each simplified into two versions and rated by radiologists and PPI readers

evidence.title: Knowledge and Awareness of Performance Metrics in Dental Image Analysis With Artificial Intelligence: A Cross-Sectional Survey of Researchers and Clinicians
evidence.outcome: Knowledge of AI performance metrics among dental researchers and clinicians
evidence.effect: Mean score 17.1% fully correct responses (SD 15.2%); theoretical questions fully correct 1%-15%; applied scenarios 17%-37% correct; errors included familiarity bias towards accuracy and task-metric misalignment.
evidence.quote: Overall performance was poor with participants achieving a mean score of 17.1% (SD: 15.2%, median: 16.7%, IQR: 16.7%) for fully correct responses.
evidence.sample_unit: survey participants (oral health researchers and clinicians)

evidence.title: Uncertainty quantification framework for AI-based survival models: Application to lung cancer prognosis in older adults for informed decision-making
evidence.outcome: Uncertainty in individual predictions despite high aggregate AUC across survival models
evidence.effect: Mean AUCs 0.840 to 0.851, yet 26% of test-set patients were assigned to conflicting risk groups depending on the model used.
evidence.quote: Although the survival models achieved high mean areas under the receiver operating characteristics curve ranging from 0.840 to 0.851, 26% of patients in the test set were assigned to conflicting risk groups depending on the model used, indicating considerable variability in model-predicted prognosis.

evidence.title: External validation of machine learning models for estimation of mortality 1, 3, 6, and 12 months after hip fracture on 5,055 consecutive patients
evidence.outcome: Whether AUC alone concealed poor calibration in mortality models
evidence.effect: Uncalibrated models had acceptable AUC but overestimated risk; calibration slope and intercept revealed miscalibration (e.g., 1-month XGB intercept -0.80), improved after recalibration.
evidence.quote: This is also evident by comparing the results and calibration curves in the present study before and after recalibration.

evidence.title: Revenue-sensitive evaluation of AI-assisted ICD-10-CM coding and human-AI collaboration under dual DRG payment systems
evidence.outcome: Metric sensitivity to operational performance
evidence.effect: AUC-micro 0.976–0.993 despite F1-micro range 0.481–0.593.
evidence.quote: Uniformly high AUC-micro scores (0.976–0.993) coexist with a wide F1-micro range (0.481–0.593): with 7942 codes per admission, the vast majority of code-admission pairs are true negatives that all models correctly identify.

evidence.title: Performance of multivariable risk prediction algorithms in predicting COPD exacerbations: a population-based study
evidence.outcome: calibration of ACCEPT 2.0
evidence.effect: ACCEPT 2.0 overpredicted: O/E ratio 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.81).
evidence.quote: However, it overpredicted exacerbation events (observed-to-expected (O/E) ratio: 0.81 (95% CI 0.80 to 0.81)).

evidence.title: Screening for Missed Opportunities for Diagnosis in the ED Using eTriggers and Large Language Models
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity-specificity tradeoffs and threshold variation across LLMs in identifying missed diagnoses
evidence.effect: Similar discrimination but different binary thresholds; 72-hour cohort sensitivity 42.9% (GPT-5 mini) to 85.7% (Claude Sonnet 4); specificity 55.9% to 82.9%.
evidence.quote: Across cohorts, LLMs showed similar discrimination but different sensitivity-specificity tradeoffs; Claude Sonnet 4 generally favored higher sensitivity, whereas GPT-5 mini favored higher specificity.

evidence.title: The Illusion of Precision: Artificial Intelligence Cannot yet Reliably Predict Individual Outcomes in Infrapopliteal Chronic Limb-Threatening Ischemia
evidence.outcome: Calibration (Brier score) versus discrimination (sensitivity) of LLM outcome predictions
evidence.effect: DS naive Brier score 0.068 at 6 months suggested high probabilistic accuracy, but all models had sensitivity 0.00 at 6-month and 1-year horizons; calibration masked discriminatory failure.
evidence.quote: However, this mathematical precision masked a failure in clinical utility: all models exhibited a sensitivity of 0.00 at 6-month and 1-year horizons.

evidence.title: Benchmarking of radiobiological NTCP models in head and neck radiotherapy using independent computational pipelines: an institutional validation study with machine learning augmentation
evidence.outcome: Majority-class accuracy under severe imbalance
evidence.effect: Accuracy 85.0%–94.1% mostly reflected predicting absence of Grade ≥2 toxicity, not clinical utility.
evidence.quote: Reported accuracy values (85.0%–94.1%) largely reflected correct classification of the majority class (absence of Grade ≥ 2 toxicity) and were therefore not interpreted as indicators of clinical utility in the context of severe class imbalance [ 51 ].

evidence.title: LLM-Generated Lay-Language Protocols for Molecular Tumor Board Patients: Evaluation of Quality and Clinical Usability
evidence.outcome: Automatic metrics versus expert safety errors
evidence.effect: A2 improved automatic metrics, but ≥1 critical error doubled for Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct: 10/25, 40% vs 5/25, 20%.
evidence.quote: However, expert usability evaluation of Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct showed the opposite picture: the proportion of protocols containing at least 1 critical error doubled under A2 (10/25, 40% vs 5/25, 20%) compared with A1, and the dominant error type shifted from language (40/108, 37%) errors to factual errors (69/145, 48%).
evidence.sample_unit: generated patient protocols (25 MTB cases x 2 prompting approaches) expert-annotated

evidence.title: Validation and Comparison of 10-Year Cardiovascular Risk Prediction Models in Two Chinese Prospective Cohorts: The General Population and Patients With Type 2 Diabetes
evidence.outcome: Calibration despite discrimination
evidence.effect: C-statistic ranges were 0.723-0.778 vs. 0.584-0.629, while original models had substantial miscalibration.
evidence.quote: Widely used 10-year CVD risk models showed acceptable or modest discrimination but substantial miscalibration in Chinese populations, especially among adults with type 2 diabetes.

evidence.title: Clinical transportability, calibration drift, and local updating of a B-mode ultrasound radiomics-clinical prediction model for occult high-volume central lymph node metastasis in cN0 papillary thyroid carcinoma: development, temporal validation, and external validation
evidence.outcome: AUC versus calibration
evidence.effect: AUC remained high, including Center 3 AUC 0.870, while Center 3 overpredicted 36.4% vs. 23.5%.
evidence.quote: In the lowest-event-rate external cohort, the locked model retained discrimination but overestimated average risk before recalibration.

evidence.title: CTest-Metric: A Unified Framework to Assess Clinical Validity of Metrics for CT Report Generation
evidence.outcome: Validity of report-generation evaluation metrics against expert ratings and under style or error perturbation
evidence.effect: Lexical NLG metrics highly sensitive to stylistic variation; GREEN Score best aligned with experts (Spearman~0.70); CRG negatively correlated; BERTScore-F1 least sensitive to factual error injection.
evidence.quote: Using our novel framework, we found that lexical NLG metrics are highly sensitive to stylistic variations; GREEN Score aligns best with expert judgments (Spearman~0.70), while CRG shows negative correlation; and BERTScore-F1 is least sensitive to factual error injection.
evidence.sample_unit: CT report cases rated by clinicians (disagreement cases)

evidence.title: IyawoBench v2.0: Extended Diagnostic Evaluation of Large Language Model Clinical Triage in Nigerian Primary Care
evidence.outcome: Whether conventional safety metrics conceal triage failure modes
evidence.effect: Models scoring 100% on binary 'did not send an emergency home' safety measures may still show systematic failure modes; sensitivity metrics conceal a 77 percentage point under-triage gap in Llama 3.1 8B.
evidence.quote: Existing safety metrics, however, produce misleading confidence: models scoring 100% on binary "did not send an emergency home" safety measures may nevertheless exhibit systematic failure modes that render them undeployable at scale.

evidence.title: Toward Better Assessment of LLMs' Performance in Clinical Error Detection
evidence.outcome: Pairwise discrimination versus aggregate F1 for LLM clinical error detection across 4 test sets and 3 languages
evidence.effect: 13 of 15 models fell below random pairwise discrimination despite moderate-looking F1 scores; F1 and pairwise accuracy move in opposite directions under the same bias, so F1 ranking may favor the weakest discriminators.
evidence.quote: In particular, evaluating 15 diverse LLMs on 4 standardized clinical error-detection test sets across 3 languages, we find that 13 of 15 models fall below the level of random pairwise discrimination, even while achieving F1 scores that standard practice would read as moderate.
evidence.sample_unit: LLMs evaluated on 4 clinical error-detection test sets

evidence.title: Algorithmic Versus Expert Rankings of Large Language Models in Peritoneal Dialysis Prescription Review: A Trap-Embedded Synthetic Benchmark
evidence.outcome: Agreement of LLM rankings across scoring constructs and with expert adequacy ratings
evidence.effect: Recall, alarm-burden proxy and WCS gave three different model orderings; WCS showed no positive association with blinded expert adequacy (rho -0.17, p=0.41) despite strong inter-rater concordance (rho 0.977).
evidence.quote: In the expert substudy, inter-rater concordance was strong (rho 0.977), but WCS did not show a positive association with expert adequacy (rho -0.17, p=0.41).
evidence.sample_unit: LLM calls (125 synthetic cases x 5 models x 3 runs)

evidence.title: Demographic Calibration Gaps in Breast Cancer Risk Prediction: Introducing the Demographic Calibration Gap Score
evidence.outcome: Reporting of calibration by subgroup and conformal coverage under shift
evidence.effect: Conformal coverage collapsed to roughly 25% on MIMIC; aggregate statistics miss subgroup calibration error, and most studies skip calibration reporting.
evidence.quote: Conformal coverage collapsed to roughly 25% on MIMIC, and racial DCG exceeded 0.15 for all 20 model-variant combinations.

evidence.title: Detection without calibration: benchmarking domestic and international large language models for quality control of Mandarin  18  F-FDG PET/CT reports
evidence.outcome: Dissociation between error-detection macro-F1 and overall-score calibration (ICC) across models
evidence.effect: Macro-F1 0.356–0.667 and ICC 0.099–0.627, weakly correlated (ρ = 0.38, p = 0.18); strongest detector Claude-Opus-4.8 (0.667) calibrated poorly (0.491).
evidence.quote: Raw detection ability does not guarantee a trustworthy score, and domestic and international models differ by deployment-relevant profile rather than by overall performance rank; both essential distinctions for performing clinical nuclear-medicine QC.

evidence.title: Single-Axis Fairness Interventions Produce Asymmetric Cross-Axis Effects in Clinical Prediction
evidence.outcome: Metric sensitivity of fairness conclusions (TPR versus AUC)
evidence.effect: The same intervention could appear successful under TPR but fail under AUC evaluation; single-metric evaluation insufficient.
evidence.quote: The same intervention could appear successful under TPR but fail under AUC evaluation.

evidence.title: When external validation isn’t enough: Simpson’s paradox, direction asymmetry, and calibration collapse in cross-continental perioperative mortality prediction
evidence.outcome: Aggregate metrics concealing within-stratum discrimination (Simpson's paradox)
evidence.effect: Simpson's paradox gap of 5.0–16.5 pp; worst case aggregate AUC 0.756 vs within-stratum 0.58–0.60.
evidence.quote: Across the eight cross-population runs, aggregate AUCs concealed substantially lower within-stratum AUCs (Simpson’s paradox gap range 5.0–16.5 pp; worst case: aggregate AUC 0.756 vs within-stratum AUCs 0.58–0.60).

evidence.title: The Independence of Discrimination and Calibration in Clinical Risk Prediction: Lessons from a Multi-Timeframe Diabetes Prediction Framework
evidence.outcome: Calibration-in-the-large versus bin-level ECE and AUC for diabetes risk model
evidence.effect: AUC 0.844 and ECE 0.006, yet predicted 8.4% vs observed 5.6% (O:E 0.66, 95% CI 0.65-0.67); ECE alone concealed 50% overprediction.
evidence.quote: Despite achieving excellent discrimination (AUC = 0.844, 95% CI: 0.840-0.848) and low bin-level calibration error (ECE = 0.006), the framework systematically overpredicted risk by 50%: mean predicted probability was 8.4% versus observed rate of 5.6% (observed-to-expected ratio = 0.66, 95% CI: 0.65-0.67).
evidence.country: Not reported (synthetic data based on UK/Finnish/US parameters)

evidence.title: Prevalence Shift and ICU Mortality Miscalibration Across Institutions
evidence.outcome: calibration versus AUROC under prevalence shift
evidence.effect: ECE correlated with prevalence difference r=0.52– 0.75, p<10−14; AUROC r=−0.03–0.22, p=0.01–0.75.
evidence.quote: Hospital-level prevalence difference explained substantial variance in Expected Calibration Error (ECE: r=0.52– 0.75, p<10−14), while the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) showed no significant correlation (r=−0.03–0.22, p=0.01–0.75).

evidence.title: Evaluating Clinical Concept Extraction and Evidence-Bounded Terminology Linking: Multisite Model Comparison and Pilot Ablation Study
evidence.outcome: metric-dependent extraction performance
evidence.effect: Automated exact-match F1 ranged 0.07-0.17; embedding-match F1 ranged 0.32-0.55.
evidence.quote: Automated exact-match F1 scores ranged from 0.07 to 0.17; embedding-match F1 was highest for MedGemma (0.55), followed by Gemma (0.53),  sci_md and SciBERT (each 0.43), and Llama 3.3 (0.32).
evidence.sample_unit: deidentified clinical notes (Study 1); 56 clinical spans (Study 2); 84 terms (Study 3)

evidence.title: Exploring Bias Assessment and Strong Calibration in AI-based Medical Risk Prediction Models
evidence.outcome: Calibration consistency across folds
evidence.effect: Brier scores differed across k-folds, indicating inconsistent calibration.
evidence.quote: Cross validation and the implementation of a paired t-test showed that Brier scores differed across k -folds, indicating inconsistencies in model calibration.

evidence.title: Gender Bias When Using Artificial Intelligence to Assess Anorexia Nervosa on Social Media: Data-Driven Study
evidence.outcome: Aggregate accuracy concealing subgroup underperformance
evidence.effect: Aggregate balanced accuracy was >87% with FNR 4-6%, but decomposing by gender showed FNR roughly twice as high for females and lower accuracy for females.
evidence.quote: Nevertheless, we observed important performance differences when decomposing such values by gender, yielding in the worst case (MLP classifier, 1 model per gender) an accuracy of 0.913 for male samples and 0.844 for female samples (relative difference of 8% accuracy).

evidence.title: Development and multicentre validation of an artificial intelligence electrocardiogram model for ventricular remodeling in repaired tetralogy of Fallot
evidence.outcome: Calibration and net benefit of uncalibrated model across sites
evidence.effect: Miscalibration at one high-AUROC site (B); uncalibrated model showed negative net benefit when all centres considered.
evidence.quote: This shows that without proper consideration of calibration, a model may be harmful compared with the current standard of care when considered in the context of clinical risk tolerance.

evidence.title: Defining operational safety in clinical artificial intelligence systems
evidence.outcome: AUC concealed operational safety
evidence.effect: AI #1 had higher AUC than AI #2 (0.928 vs. 0.882) but at α=100% cleared 167 cases (16.7%) versus AI #2's 290 (29.0%).
evidence.quote: Although AI Solution #1 demonstrated a higher AUC than AI Solution #2 (0.928 vs. 0.882; Fig. 3a , b ), this advantage translated to better operational efficiency only for less stringent tasks, as evidenced by its more rapid Gray Zone reduction at moderate safety levels ( α < 95%; Fig. 3c ).

evidence.title: Real-world performance of open-source large language models in diabetes diagnosis
evidence.outcome: minority diabetes subtype errors
evidence.effect: DeepSeek-V3 Chinese Prompt 1 had weighted F1 0.951; GDM 61% and SD 42% were misclassified as T2DM.
evidence.quote: A confusion matrix analysis revealed the top-performing model (DeepSeek-V3, Chinese Prompt 1) suffered from significant class imbalance, misclassifying high proportions of minority classes like GDM (61%) and SD (42%) as T2DM.

evidence.title: Deep Learning Model Using Transfer Learning for Detecting Left Ventricular Systolic Dysfunction: Retrospective Algorithm Development and Validation Study
evidence.outcome: Whether subgroup AUROC reveals threshold-based performance degradation
evidence.effect: Subgroup AUROC remained moderately high while specificity fell sharply (LBBB AUROC 0.859, specificity 0.219), concealing threshold-level underperformance.
evidence.quote: However, the decline in specificity was considerably more pronounced than would be anticipated from AUROC alone.

evidence.title: Optimising Retraining Frequency for a Paediatric Emergency Department Admission Prediction Model: Development and Temporal Validation Using Real-World Data
evidence.outcome: Whether discrimination metrics conceal calibration degradation
evidence.effect: Static model AUROC declined modestly (0.852 to 0.799) while AMDBE rose from 2.73 to 10.6; AMDBE showed variability even when AUROC appeared stable.
evidence.quote: AMDBE expressed more concept drift than traditionally reported measures such as AUROC, sensitivity and specificity.

evidence.title: Predicting future dementia from routine clinical MRI and linked healthcare data
evidence.outcome: Reporting of uncertainty (confidence intervals) for performance metrics
evidence.effect: Confidence intervals were not estimated; only fold-level variability was reported, and no subgroup calibration was reported.
evidence.quote: Confidence intervals were not estimated due to the nested cross validation framework; however, variability across outer folds is reported to provide an indication of model stability and uncertainty.

evidence.title: Evaluation Framework for Bruise Detection: Systematic ALS/White-Light Training and Skin-Tone Balancing with Deep Learning
evidence.outcome: Sensitivity of detection performance to confidence and IoU thresholds
evidence.effect: At confidence 0.1/IoU 0.1 F1 was 0.036 vs 0.387 at 0.3/0.3; confidence >=0.7 caused near-zero detections and severe recall collapse.
evidence.quote: Notably, confidence thresholds above 0.7 result in almost no detections, and IoU thresholds greater than 0.5 significantly degrade performance.

evidence.title: A Reproducible Protocol and Framework for Large Language Model (LLM)-Assisted Estrogen and Progesterone Receptor (ER/PR) Scoring
evidence.outcome: Use of confidence intervals and appropriate metrics in reporting concordance
evidence.effect: Only simple percentage agreement reported; no Cohen's kappa, confidence intervals, or sensitivity/specificity per tier were calculated.
evidence.quote: Formal statistical measures, such as Cohen's kappa or confidence intervals, were not calculated given the feasibility study design and sample size.

evidence.title: Cross-Sensor and Cross-Population Generalization of Deep Learning Models for Digital Mammography: A Controlled Four-Country Benchmark of Five Backbone Architectures with Statistical Significance Testing
evidence.outcome: Calibration deterioration hidden by discrimination metrics at transfer
evidence.effect: Mammo-CLIP ECE on CMMD reached 0.403 and DINOv2 on MIAS 0.446, versus 0.055-0.105 in-distribution.
evidence.quote: Mammo-CLIP’s ECE on CMMD reaches 0.403, meaning its predicted probabilities are on average 40 percentage points off from the actual prevalence after distribution shift.
evidence.sample_unit: validation images (CBIS-DDSM; external: CMMD 1032, DMID 509, MIAS 322)

evidence.title: Opportunistic Osteoporosis Screening from Routine Knee Radiographs Using a Multi-Stage CNN Framework with External Validation
evidence.outcome: Discrimination (AUC) masking poor calibration and threshold-based performance
evidence.effect: High external AUC (0.87–0.89) masked poor threshold-based accuracy (~42–43%); subgroup/class-specific Osteopenia sensitivity was near zero.
evidence.quote: Importantly, high discrimination performance should not be interpreted as evidence of clinical readiness.
evidence.sample_unit: knee radiographs (116 patients internal; 150 external Kaggle images)

evidence.title: Tipping the balance: impact of class imbalance correction on the performance of clinical risk prediction models
evidence.venue: Journal of the American Medical Informatics Association : JAMIA
evidence.outcome: Discrimination versus calibration metrics after class-imbalance resampling
evidence.effect: ROC-AUC change -0.002 to -0.01; Brier scores increased 0.029-0.080 with marked calibration intercept and slope deviations, so rank-based metrics alone hid distorted predicted risks.
evidence.quote: The consistent dissociation between discrimination and calibration highlights that rank-based metrics alone are insufficient for evaluating clinical utility.

evidence.title: Algorithmovigilance in AI-Based Oral-Health Surveillance: Temporal Drift, Cross-Survey Differences, and Predictor-Level Structural Stability in Population-Level Severe Tooth Loss Prediction
evidence.outcome: Calibration instability missed by discrimination alone
evidence.effect: Observed/expected ratio declined 1.0061 to 0.7893; CITL shifted 0.0097 to −0.3645; ECE increased 0.0069 to 0.0352.
evidence.quote: Expanded calibration metrics showed that calibration instability was more apparent than discrimination change alone: the observed/expected ratio declined from 1.0061 in BRFSS 2016 to 0.7893 in BRFSS 2024, CITL shifted from 0.0097 to −0.3645, and ECE increased from 0.0069 to 0.0352.

evidence.title: How data drift impacts the safety and interpretability of machine learning models predicting risk from blood glucose control
evidence.outcome: Whether a single performance metric conceals poor performance under drift
evidence.effect: AUROC alone missed a significant sensitivity drop at +20 mg/dL shift; 'above range' AUROC rose while AP and sensitivity fell.
evidence.quote: This highlights the danger of using performance metrics alone to identify drift.
evidence.sample_unit: adults with type 1 diabetes (REPLACE trial CGM data)

evidence.title: Integrating Clinical Priorities into the Technical Validation of Machine Learning Classifiers: A Generalizable Framework Demonstrated on Opioid Misuse Screening
evidence.outcome: high raw accuracy concealing poor positive class detection
evidence.effect: CSBT-Untuned achieved 86.7% raw accuracy but missed 61.5% of positive cases (sensitivity 38.5%, 139 false negatives)
evidence.quote: The results demonstrate that while CSBT-Untuned achieved the highest raw accuracy of 86.7%, it missed 61.5% of positive cases.
evidence.sample_unit: survey respondents in the held-out test set (NSDUH 2015-2019)

commentary.bottom_line: Twelve offline or benchmark studies suggest that aggregate metrics such as AUC or Dice can hide subgroup miscalibration, poor boundary accuracy, and threshold-dependent failures that output-appropriate, subgroup, and threshold-based metrics reveal. No study tested whether adopting these metrics in evaluation changes deployment decisions or patient outcomes.

perspectives.view: Eleven of twelve tests favor the practice, and one is mixed. All are level 4 or 5 retrospective, simulated, or benchmark designs. They measure whether a metric exposes hidden differences, which is a surrogate outcome. Results are consistent, but indirectness and small or unreported samples lower certainty to low.

In lung screening, models with AUCs of 0.91 to 0.95 predicted 11% risk where 22% was observed in the highest tier. In mammography, two models with AUC 0.960 had gray zone areas of 0.709 and 0.344. These results suggest that calibration and operating-point checks may catch under-prediction that aggregate discrimination misses.

Hausdorff distance correlated with clinician editing time (Spearman 0.70) better than Dice. One study found acceptable Dice with Hausdorff distance near 20.0 mm in liver and spleen, and another found per-organ boundary metrics reshuffled rankings by 10-13%. Label-specific thresholds raised specificity from 0.844 to 0.885 but lowered macro-F1 from 0.738 to 0.693, a tradeoff teams must justify.

A subgroup false-negative audit at the deployed threshold flagged 96% of installed failures, compared with 73% for a rank-based audit, while aggregate AUROC moved 0.004. A surgical study found an aggregate AUC of 0.756 alongside within-stratum AUCs of 0.58 to 0.60. Both findings suggest that subgroup reporting may expose disparities that aggregate figures hide.

FDA draft guidance asks that validation address each output by type. A review of 691 FDA-cleared devices found that premarket summaries reported sensitivity for 24.0% and specificity for 22.0%. That hazard finding shows a reporting gap. It does not show that the recommended metrics close it.

In one study, raw accuracy ranked a model highest at 0.867, yet that model detected 38.5% of misuse cases, and bootstrap confidence intervals showed the top two balanced models overlapped. A hazard study found that the choice of threshold changed detected complication rates from 9.14% to 17.1%. No study measured the staff time or cost of this evaluation work.

In a smartwatch atrial fibrillation study, excluding inconclusive readings gave 96.1% sensitivity, while counting them gave 78.1%. How results are reported can therefore change the performance that patients and clinicians are told to expect from a device.

commentary.research_gap: No study compared deployment decisions, clinician behavior, or patient outcomes between evaluations that used subgroup calibration, confidence intervals, and justified thresholds and evaluations that relied on aggregate metrics. Prospective or stepped implementation studies in live settings would be needed to show whether the practice prevents harm.
commentary.underserved_note: One test of the practice focused on racial and ethnic minority subgroups. No test included Medicaid, safety-net, limited English proficiency, or low-literacy populations, so the evidence cannot show whether these metrics detect underperformance in those groups, where small subgroup samples may also widen confidence intervals.
